extracted.intended_audience: British statesmen, legislators, and educated public concerned with the French Revolution and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: A political-philosophical critique of revolutionary confiscation and wholesale institutional reform, offering normative criteria for assessing when and how governments may alter property, corporations, and public institutions. Aimed at guiding statesmen and public opinion about prudence, justice, and the preservation-or-reform balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for prescription and property
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The rules of prescription are part of the law of Nature... If prescription be once shaken, no species of property is secure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that prescription (long possession and legal usage) secures property; undermining prescription endangers all forms of property when they become tempting to concentrated power. Examples drawn from French confiscations and warning that once legal protections are overturned, nothing is safe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative assemblies have no right to violate property
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Parliaments had any right whatever to violate property, to overrule prescription, or to force a currency of their own fiction' — assemblies sitting 'not for the security, but for the destruction of property.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts a normative limit on legislative power: assemblies should not set aside established property rights or impose fictitious currencies; doing so is presented as illegitimate even if the act could not be sustained in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confiscation is a dangerous and unjust policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Confiscation of estates (church or otherwise) sets a precedent of injustice and invites broader plunder: 'Revolutions are favorable to confiscation... it is impossible to know under what obnoxious names the next confiscations will be authorized.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains political and social dangers: encourages unrest among the moneyed interest, destabilizes trust in government, and may provoke search for new, more energetic regimes founded on contempt of justice. Cites French practice as leading progressively from clergy to nobility to all property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy must be grounded in justice and public benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Justice is itself the great standing policy of civil society; and any eminent departure from it, under any circumstances, lies under the suspicion of being no policy at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that alleged 'policy' cannot justify a clear breach of justice; abolition or confiscation must show evident and significant public benefit, not only speculative or hortatory reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer preservation and improvement over wholesale abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Spartam nactus es; hanc exorna' — where institutions have roots, one should adorn and improve them rather than destroy them outright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for a middle course between absolute destruction and unreformed existence: preserve useful parts and fit reforms to what remains, making 'the most of the existing materials' of a country rather than treating it as a blank slate.

rubrics_metrics.name: A true statesman combines disposition to preserve with ability to improve
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A disposition to preserve, and an ability to improve, taken together, would be my standard of a statesman.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for political actors: not mere radicalism or mere conservationism, but the combination of reverence for existing valuable structures and competence to reform them practically and prudently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawgivers should be deliberate, sensitive, and cautious
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The true lawgiver ought to have a heart full of sensibility... movements towards [the goal] ought to be deliberate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of rash, experimental legislation. Emphasizes moral sensibility, fear of harming people by sudden alteration of their state and habits, and that circumspection and caution are duties when altering social institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confront difficulty rather than evade it
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform that preserves-and-improves requires 'a vigorous mind, steady, persevering attention, various powers of comparison and combination, and the resources of an understanding fruitful in expedients' — not evasion of difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts constructive reform (hard work, confronting obstacles) with facile destruction (easy to abolish what exists). Points out that avoiding difficulty leads to weak, ill-considered institutions that multiply problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of fanaticism and proselytism as political threats
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The spirit of atheistical fanaticism... has filled the populace with a black and savage atrocity of mind' and proselytism organizes to propagate discontent across countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical examples (Anabaptists of Munster) and contemporary French street preaching to warn that fanatic zeal can erode moral sentiments, produce social violence, and export revolutionary disorder internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and preserve the unique public value of corporate institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Monastic and corporate bodies 'were found a great power for the mechanism of politic benevolence' — revenues with public direction, men dedicated to public purposes, permanence suited to long-term projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues these corporations provide disciplined manpower, stable revenues, libraries, collections, monuments and other public goods that scattered private purchasers may not secure. Destroying them wastes instruments of long-term public utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare current possessors with prospective purchasers before transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Before confiscation and sale, a legislator should compare the existing possessor with the proposed new holder to judge who better returns the surplus to industry and public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists criteria for comparison: industriousness, virtue, sobriety, tendency to expend surpluses productively (e.g., libraries, collections, monuments) vs. wasteful consumption; warns against assuming purchasers will be superior stewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute speculative symbols for real currency and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They have compelled all men... to accept, as perfect payment and good and lawful tender, the symbols of their speculations on a projected sale of their plunder.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that forcing acceptance of depreciated or speculative paper undermines commerce, circulation, and trust; such monetary fiction substitutes threaten economic stability and international standing.
